messages.subject: map per row
parts:
I often need to run simple map transforms on each row of a data frame, creating a data frame with the same number of rows.  Given the first column is unique and called "id": 

id x y z
1  1 2 3
3  4 5 6
5  7 8 9

the plyr call looks like

res <- daply(df, .(id), function(row) with(row, data.frame(x / y, x / z))

It takes a while on long data frames.  Is daply optimized to be on par with apply/lapply in this case, and what other R ways are there to get a fast, yet cute-looking, map like this?

Cheers,
Alexy

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: map per row
parts:
Hi:

Your code returns a list, but you evidently want a matrix. Therefore,
your function should return a numeric vector rather than a data frame,
as follows:

> u <- daply(df, .(id), function(d) with(d, c(xy = x/y, xz = x/z)))
> u

id xy xz
1 0.500 0.3333333
3 0.800 0.6666667
5 0.875 0.7777778

One of the keys to understanding how the **ply() functions work is to
make sure, whenever possible, that the input argument of the function
you want to pass has the same class as the input class (here d =
data.frame) and the output of the function has the same class as the
output class (a = array, which covers numeric vectors (1D), matrices
(2D) or arrays (>= 2D)).

An exception to this rule may apply when inputting or outputting
lists; in that event, the class of the input argument is that of a
generic list component if one is reading from a list, whereas the
output should conform to the output class (perhaps that of a generic
list component if a list is the output class). These little nuances in
plyr can drive you up the wall if you're not alert :)

This should be significantly faster than your version because data
frames have a lot of overhead, but if it's still not fast enough, then
look into the data.table package. For this problem, you'd do the
following:

library('data.table')
# convert a data frame to a data table
> dt <- data.table(df)
# output the (list) of two named variables xy and xz as defined
# the initial comma after the left bracket is not a typo.
> dt[, list(xy = x/y, xz = x/z)]
xy xz
[1,] 0.500 0.3333333
[2,] 0.800 0.6666667
[3,] 0.875 0.7777778

HTH,
Dennis
